content: Why do Ozempic and Wegovy help some people lose remarkable amounts of weight while others see disappointing results? Scientists are investigating whether the body’s natural tendency to conserve energy during weight loss could be an overlooked piece of the puzzle. Medications like Ozempic and Wegovy, which contain semaglutide — a GLP‑1 receptor agonist that helps regulate blood sugar, appetite, and body weight — have become household names and important pillars in obesity management for the medical profession. Research has shown GLP-1 medications reduce body weight by an average of 15 percent when used weekly for 68 weeks and combined with lifestyle interventions. This is because semaglutide acts on the brain to increase the feeling of fullness and to decrease appetite. These medications don’t work the same way for everyone, however. Our multidisciplinary research team at the University of Alberta is working to improve obesity care for people of all ages and to understand why some people respond better to semaglutide than others, and how their weight loss can be maintained over time. We are investigating the role of energy metabolism as a potentially important piece in a complex puzzle. Research has shown that semaglutide medications can improve quality of life, blood markers such as sugar and cholesterol, strength, and overall health. Weight loss is only one measure of how well they work. We are exploring whether people’s responses to these medications could lie in individual factors such as genetics, metabolism, body composition, lifestyle, microbiota, associated diseases, age, and sex. Energy metabolism may also be an important piece of this puzzle. This is a measure of the total calories consumed (in) and the total calories burned (out). We burn calories all the time: for vital processes like breathing and thinking, physical activities like going to the gym, and the everyday act of digesting food. When we lose weight, our bodies naturally need less energy. But sometimes, the body goes into an extra “energy-saving mode,” burning even fewer calories than we would expect. This is called metabolic adaptation, or adaptive thermogenesis . Think of it like a light bulb that automatically dims to save electricity. This is one reason why losing weight can become more difficult over time, sometimes leading to a weight-loss plateau. Changes in body weight and composition (the amount of fat and fat-free mass in our bodies) play an important role in energy metabolism. Both fat and fat-free mass use energy, even when we are resting. As we lose these tissues, our bodies naturally burn fewer calories. Researchers are still trying to understand whether weight-loss medications influence these processes differently. If we can understand how our bodies use energy during and after weight loss, this could help us develop better strategies for maintaining weight loss over the long term. We published a recent review of studies investigating the effects of GLP-1 therapies on energy utilization . We found a few studies exploring how semaglutide affects resting energy use, with findings that were neutral or inconclusive. The question of how semaglutide impacts energy use is an emerging area of study and remains an open question for exploration. At the University of Alberta, we have a gold-standard method to measure energy utilization called a whole-room indirect calorimeter . This is a rare research facility and is similar to a hotel suite that can precisely measure each component of energy use . This room can isolate the effects of changes in someone’s calorie burning at rest, after eating, and during exercise. We are currently recruiting research participants with blood sugar regulation issues, such as insulin resistance or diabetes, who are about to start semaglutide treatment. We will follow their weight-loss journey over six months to investigate changes in body weight and composition and energy utilization using sophisticated approaches. Understanding how semaglutide influences energy use and body composition, and how these changes interact, could be an important step toward explaining why individuals respond differently to weight-loss treatment. This will allow us to contribute to more personalized approaches to obesity and Type 2 diabetes management in the future. Having a better understanding of how energy use changes with semaglutide-induced weight loss will also help us to better anticipate potential non-responders (people who do not lose weight) and offer alternative treatments sooner in their health journey. Importantly, current evidence suggests that if you are taking semaglutide or considering starting treatment, you should make a few lifestyle changes. These include improving your nutrition by increasing protein intake and prioritizing fresh foods , such as fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins like fish and poultry , nuts, and seeds. It’s important to eat small portions at consistent times throughout the day, avoid skipping meals, pay attention to your hunger and fullness cues, and choose water as your beverage of choice. It’s also recommended to engage in resistance exercise to support muscle and bone health and achieve the best results. These strategies may help limit reductions in energy use as the weight comes off. Written by: Adapted from an article originally published in The Conversation . content: New research is challenging how scientists understand cerebral palsy (CP). Of 515 genes previously linked to the condition, only 89 showed a statistically significant association in a new study, suggesting that many proposed genetic connections still lack sufficient evidence. Published in the journal American Journal of Human Genetics , the research also proposes a different way to classify CP. Rather than treating it as a single disorder, the scientists suggest it may be better understood as a collection of symptoms arising from multiple underlying conditions. Cerebral palsy is the most common motor disability in children, with up to 10,000 babies diagnosed in the United States annually. It has traditionally been associated with complications around birth, including premature delivery and temporary oxygen deprivation. However, genetic research over the past decade has increasingly pointed to inherited or newly occurring genetic variants as potential contributors. Unlike progressive neurological diseases, CP does not worsen over time, and rehabilitation and physical therapy can improve symptoms. “There has been a lack of consensus on the definition of cerebral palsy and on the role of genetics in disease pathogenesis, leading to substantial variability in whether a child is diagnosed with CP,” says corresponding author Peter Robinson of the Jackson Laboratory for Genomic Medicine and the Berlin Institute of Health at Charité. “We have developed a paradigm that considers CP to be a phenotypic trait rather than a precise disease diagnosis. A better understanding of specific genetic variants has the potential to improve our understanding of the biology of the disease.” To investigate the genetic basis of CP, the researchers evaluated evidence from 21 previously published studies involving 5,440 people diagnosed with the condition. These studies had identified potentially causal variants across hundreds of genes, but the new statistical analysis found convincing evidence of association for only a fraction of them. “We decided to do this study because there has been no accepted statistical method to determine if a disease-associated gene is truly linked to CP,” says first author Adam Arterbery of the Jackson Laboratory for Genomic Medicine. “We discovered it was extremely difficult to find statistical evidence of causality for many of the genetic variants previously linked to CP.” The team also performed whole-genome sequencing on 460 children from 453 families receiving care at Shriners Children’s hospitals across the United States. Pathogenic or likely pathogenic genetic variants were identified in 70 families, spanning 60 genes. However, just 16 of those genes overlapped with the genes supported by statistically significant evidence in the analysis of earlier studies. The researchers emphasize that their findings do not disprove connections between CP and the remaining genes. Instead, the available data are insufficient to establish those associations with statistical confidence. They propose viewing CP as a clinical characteristic that can emerge from different genetic disorders and environmental influences, rather than a single disease with a common biological origin. “This framework could improve interpretation of genomic testing, help identify children who may warrant closer CP surveillance or specialist referral, and potentially identify genetic conditions requiring disease-specific management,” Robinson says. “But clinical utility and patient benefit will absolutely need validation before these findings can be applied to patient care.” Future studies will focus on larger patient populations, prospective evaluations of clinical benefits and costs, and better access to genomic and medical data. “We hope our study will stimulate discussion about CP terminology, gene-disease associations, and variant interpretation,” Arterbery says. “The most productive response will be further validation and development of better genotype-phenotype evidence rather than treating the findings as a definitive list of CP genes.” Reference: “A phenotypic paradigm for cerebral palsy genetics” by Adam S. content: For children with ADHD, the support they receive at school may not always make the difference parents and teachers hope for. Giving children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) more time to finish assignments, frequent breaks, or a quieter place to work might seem like straightforward ways to help them succeed in school. These adjustments are widely used in classrooms, yet new research suggests they may do little to improve academic performance or behavior. A study from Florida International University (FIU) , published in JAMA Pediatrics , found that four common accommodations did not produce significant improvements in children with ADHD. The results raise questions about how schools support students whose difficulties with attention, behavior, and completing schoolwork can interfere with their education. “We were surprised that none of the accommodations we tested had a significant effect, even when combined with behavioral interventions or medication,” said Gregory Fabiano, a psychology professor at FIU and the study’s lead author. Researchers at FIU’s Center for Children and Families conducted a randomized clinical trial involving 255 children with ADHD, ranging from kindergarten through sixth grade. The children entered the study between 2022 and 2025, and 235 completed it. The research took place through FIU’s Summer Treatment Program , which provides structured classroom and recreational activities for children with ADHD. Researchers tested four accommodations commonly offered in schools: extended time on assignments, frequent breaks, standing while working at a desk, and completing work in a low-distraction environment. They measured how these adjustments affected classroom rule violations, academic productivity, and quiz scores under different treatment conditions. The results revealed clear differences between the commonly used accommodations and treatments designed to address ADHD symptoms: The distinction matters because schools frequently include accommodations in Individualized Education Programs (IEPs) and Section 504 plans, which are designed to meet students’ individual educational needs. Although these adjustments may make classroom tasks more manageable for some children, the findings suggest that routinely providing them does not necessarily improve measurable academic outcomes or behavior. “These approaches fail to build skills or address motivation,” Fabiano said. Rather than relying heavily on accommodations, researchers recommend placing greater emphasis on behavioral strategies supported by evidence. These include setting clear expectations, providing consistent feedback, praising positive behavior, and rewarding students for meeting personalized goals. One approach is the use of daily report cards, which allow teachers to monitor specific behaviors and give students regular feedback on their progress. The findings do not mean accommodations are never useful. Individual students may benefit from particular adjustments, even if those approaches did not produce significant improvements across the children studied. “There may be times when accommodations may be helpful, but a ‘one size fits all’ approach to ADHD doesn’t seem to be effective,” he said. The research builds on decades of work by the late William E. Pelham Jr., the founding director of FIU’s Center for Children and Families, who helped design and conduct the study. A pioneer in ADHD treatment, Pelham also led landmark research showing that stimulant medication improved children’s classroom productivity without significantly improving how much they learned. That earlier finding highlights an important distinction between helping students complete schoolwork and helping them understand and retain information. The latest study also has limitations. Researchers conducted the trial in structured summer treatment classrooms rather than ordinary schools, where classroom conditions, teaching practices, and available support may differ. Additional research is needed to determine whether the results hold in everyday educational settings. For Fabiano, the findings underscore the need to reconsider which forms of support schools prioritize for children with ADHD. “We need to rethink how we’re supporting these students, with greater emphasis on effective treatments in everyday classrooms rather than relying so heavily on accommodations. Every child with ADHD deserves the opportunity to succeed and feel proud of what they’ve accomplished in the classroom, and it is our job to make sure we give them the best chance for that,” Fabiano said. Reference: “Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Accommodations, Behavior Therapy, and Stimulant Medication: A Randomized Clinical Trial” by Gregory A. Fabiano, Brittany M. Merrill, Rosalia F.
